question: A 38-year-old chronic alcohol user is brought to casualty confused and tremulous. His last drink was 18 hours ago. Blood glucose is 48 mg/dL. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Giving glucose first without thiamine in a chronic alcohol user risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy by exhausting residual thiamine reserves. Always give thiamine BEFORE glucose.

answers.text: Administer IV thiamine 100 mg first, then correct hypoglycaemia with dextrose.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Chronic alcohol use depletes thiamine. Glucose administration before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. The sequence thiamine → then glucose is mandatory.

answers.text: Start chlordiazepoxide 25 mg orally and monitor the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment score.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Benzodiazepines are the correct treatment for alcohol withdrawal seizure prevention, but the immediate clinical emergency here is hypoglycaemia. The metabolic threat must be corrected first — with thiamine preceding glucose.

answers.text: Obtain a urine drug screen before initiating any treatment.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Investigations should not delay treatment in an acute emergency. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia requires immediate correction; wait for lab results only after stabilisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the alcohol withdrawal emergency timeline. In chronic alcohol users with hypoglycaemia, IV thiamine must precede glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Well done. The thiamine-before-glucose rule is a life-saving sequence in alcohol-dependent patients. Memorise it: T → G.
